This study introduces a novel time-varying Poisson auto-regressive model with exogenous covariates, termed the Time-Varying Poisson PARX (TV-PARX). Unlike conventional Poisson PARX models, which assume static parameters, the TV-PARX framework allows for nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in the data. We establish the consistency of the least squares estimator and derive its asymptotic distribution. Furthermore, we introduce a data-driven method for selecting the optimal number of lags in the TV-PARX model. Simulation results and an analysis of real-world data demonstrate that the TV-PARX model effectively captures nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks, outperforming standard Poisson PARX models and other competing approaches. These findings suggest that the TV-PARX model is a valuable tool for forecasting count time series characterized by nonlinear behaviors and structural shifts. To facilitate practical application, we have made the R implementation of the TV-PARX model available at https://github.com/chenyuxia/TV-PARX.

This study introduces a method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau_{\rm A}$) using wide-field photometry, a technique that does not require absolute calibration. The approach relies on the fact that the intensity of starlight varies with the zenith angle due to atmospheric extinction. By analyzing the light curves of stars observed across a wide field of view, we can derive the extinction coefficient and, consequently, $\tau_{\rm A}$. We applied this method to data collected by the 1.0-meter telescope at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile, utilizing the $I$-band photometry from the ALMA Photometric Camera (APCam). The resulting $\tau_{\rm A}$ values were compared with those from a standard method that uses a calibrated star as a reference. The two datasets showed good agreement, with a root-mean-square difference of 0.01. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between $\tau_{\rm A}$ and the aerosol fine-mode fraction (FMF), finding that the data aligns with the seasonal variations in FMF reported by the AERONET network. This confirms that the proposed method is effective for monitoring atmospheric conditions at ALMA. Additionally, the technique could be valuable for other astronomical facilities employing wide-field photometric cameras, such as the Atacama Large Aperture Submillimeter Telescope (LAST), which is currently under construction in Chile.

This study introduces a novel numerical approach for integrating Langevin dynamics, termed the fractional Adams-Bashforth (FAB) method. Unlike conventional schemes that rely on fixed time steps, the FAB method employs a variable time step strategy. We demonstrate that the FAB scheme maintains high accuracy and stability even with large time steps, outperforming standard methods like the velocity Verlet (VV) and fractional Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (FABM) in both precision and computational speed. To validate these findings, we conducted simulations of the alanine dipeptide using the FAB, VV, and FABM methods. Results indicate that the FAB method achieves comparable accuracy to the VV and FABM schemes while requiring significantly less computational time. Furthermore, we analyzed the impact of the time step on the root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) of the backbone atoms in the alanine dipeptide. Our analysis reveals that the FAB method remains stable and accurate even with a large time step of 0.005 ps, whereas the VV and FABM methods exhibit instability and reduced accuracy under the same conditions. These results suggest that the FAB method is a promising candidate for simulating biomolecular systems, offering a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. By enabling the use of larger time steps, this approach could facilitate the investigation of rare events in biomolecular dynamics. The source code for the FAB method is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyongqiang/FAB.

Although image description systems have been extensively studied, the creation of high-quality datasets for this task remains a significant challenge. While numerous datasets exist, they often lack the detailed, precise, and comprehensive descriptions necessary for visually impaired users to fully understand images. Furthermore, existing guidelines for generating image descriptions are either absent or insufficient. To address these issues, we introduce a new dataset, ImageDescriptionGuidelines, which pairs images with detailed descriptions and corresponding guidelines. Additionally, we present a set of comprehensive guidelines for creating image descriptions, which we have incorporated into the new dataset. To evaluate the effectiveness of these guidelines, we developed an automatic evaluation metric, ImageDescriptionGuidelinesMetric, and a corresponding model, ImageDescriptionGuidelinesModel, designed to assess the quality of generated descriptions against the guidelines. We also created a new dataset, ImageDescriptionGuidelinesTest, to validate this metric and model. Experimental results indicate that our metric and model outperform current state-of-the-art automatic evaluation methods. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating our guidelines into training data significantly enhances the performance of image description generation models. The new dataset, guidelines, metric, and model are publicly available at https://github.com/ahmadreza1377/ImageDescriptionGuidelines. Our contributions include: (1) a new dataset featuring images, detailed descriptions, and associated guidelines; (2) a comprehensive set of guidelines for generating image descriptions; (3) an automatic evaluation metric and model for assessing generated descriptions against these guidelines; (4) a new dataset for validating the metric and model; and (5) evidence showing that integrating our guidelines into training data improves image description generation models. These resources are accessible at https://github.com/ahmadreza1377/ImageDescriptionGuidelines.

The resulting formula is expressed using Nielsen generalized polylogarithms. To achieve this, we developed a Python package named "EulerOpt," which implements the proposed optimization strategy. The source code for EulerOpt is publicly accessible at https://github.com/AndreaFaccini/EulerOpt. Finally, we outline potential future extensions of this methodology.

The objective of optimization is to minimize the complexity of these tensor products. This is achieved by expressing the tensor products as linear combinations of a set of basis integrals, thereby reducing the complexity of the associated coefficient functions.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework for fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) at a specific scale, incorporating uncertainties arising from both experimental data and the DGLAP evolution process. The methodology involves constructing a prior distribution for PDFs at a reference scale by utilizing a set of data points and their associated uncertainties. Subsequently, the posterior distribution at the target scale is derived by combining this prior with a likelihood function that quantifies the discrepancy between evolved PDFs and the observed data. To address the computational challenge of evolving a large number of PDF parameters, we employ a neural network to approximate the DGLAP evolution operator. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through a Monte Carlo analysis of a simplified model, where the results align with expectations. Furthermore, the method is applied to fit NNPDF2.3 PDFs at the scale $\mu=2$ GeV, yielding a posterior distribution that closely resembles the original prior. Finally, we explore the potential for reducing uncertainties in the fitted PDFs by incorporating additional data points. This work represents the first attempt to integrate the DGLAP evolution uncertainty into a Bayesian PDF fitting framework. The proposed methodology offers a viable pathway for including other sources of uncertainty in future PDF fitting efforts. Furthermore, the neural network approximation of the DGLAP evolution operator can be adapted for other applications, such as Monte Carlo simulations of LHC events. Ultimately, this approach provides a practical solution for managing the computational demands associated with the DGLAP evolution operator.

Neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) serves as a sensitive probe for physics beyond the Standard Model, potentially revealing the origin of neutrino mass and confirming that neutrinos are Majorana particles. The decay rate is governed by the product of a short-range nuclear matrix element (NME) and a long-range neutrino potential. While the NME is typically calculated using nuclear many-body theories, the neutrino potential relies on two-body currents, which are derived from the same underlying physics responsible for single beta decay. Consequently, the neutrino potential is intrinsically linked to the axial form factor, a quantity that remains uncertain at the low momentum transfers relevant to $0\nu\beta\beta$. This paper presents a novel approach to determining the neutrino potential by employing a neural network to model the axial form factor. We validate this method using data from pion and eta decays, as well as neutrino-nucleon scattering. Our findings indicate that the neural network approach yields a neutrino potential consistent with existing literature.

Neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (NS-LMXBs) represent the final evolutionary stage of a specific subset of millisecond radio pulsars (MSPs), which are themselves the end product of a binary system where the neutron star accretes matter from a companion star. While the total number of MSPs in the Galaxy is well established, the population of NS-LMXBs remains uncertain due to the difficulty in detecting faint systems. This study utilizes a sample of 1200 MSPs from the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array to identify potential NS-LMXBs by searching for transient X-ray emissions. The analysis reveals that approximately 10% of the MSP population exhibits transient X-ray activity, corresponding to a total Galactic NS-LMXB population of roughly 10,000. These findings suggest that the majority of MSPs have not yet transitioned into the NS-LMXB phase, implying that the current NS-LMXB population is insufficient to account for the observed millisecond radio pulsar population. Consequently, the existence of a substantial population of ultracompact MSP binaries—systems with short orbital periods that are currently undetectable—is required to explain the overall MSP distribution. This conclusion aligns with recent results from the NICER mission, which indicate that the population of ultracompact NS-LMXBs is significantly larger than previously estimated. Furthermore, this work provides the first direct evidence that the population of ultracompact MSP binaries is dominated by systems containing millisecond neutron stars. These results offer crucial insights into the formation mechanisms of ultracompact binaries and the evolution of MSPs within the Galaxy. Additionally, the study suggests that the population of ultracompact MSP binaries may be substantial enough to serve as a viable source of gravitational waves detectable by future space-based observatories. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of multi-messenger astronomy in uncovering the origins of ultracompact binaries and the evolutionary pathways of MSPs.

Finally, we introduce a method for calculating the crossing number of a diagonal knot and provide a lower bound for the crossing number of conventional knots. As an application of these results, we derive a new lower bound for the crossing number of torus knots. These findings offer valuable insights into the design of multi-agent systems and the development of effective task allocation mechanisms. To address these issues, we introduce a hybrid model that integrates $N$-gram models with neural networks. Specifically, we propose a novel neural architecture that incorporates an $N$-gram embedding layer, which converts $N$-gram features into a dense embedding space. This embedding is then processed by a transformer-based neural language model. We evaluate this hybrid approach on two tasks: machine translation and automatic question answering. Our results demonstrate that incorporating $N$-gram features into the neural architecture yields substantial performance gains. For instance, in machine translation, our model surpasses the state-of-the-art by 0.3 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-to-French dataset and by 0.2 BLEU points on the IWSLT14 German-to-English dataset. These findings confirm that combining $N$-gram models with neural networks is an effective strategy for enhancing language tasks. Teacher-Student architectures have emerged as a primary strategy for creating lightweight student networks that match the performance of deeper teacher networks. While these models have been extensively studied, their efficacy in scenarios where the teacher network is itself lightweight remains underexplored. This work introduces a novel framework for designing lightweight student networks that surpass the performance of their corresponding lightweight teacher networks. Our approach involves a two-stage process: first, we develop a lightweight teacher network by integrating a lightweight convolutional block into a standard teacher architecture; second, we train a student network to replicate the features of this lightweight teacher. To optimize the student's ability to mimic the teacher, we introduce a new loss function that leverages the feature maps of an intermediate convolutional block. Extensive experiments on ImageNet and COCO datasets demonstrate that our method, termed Light-Student, significantly outperforms existing techniques. Specifically, on ImageNet, Light-Student surpasses the current state-of-the-art by 1.1% in top-1 accuracy for a 2MB model and by 1.5% for a 4MB model. Furthermore, on COCO, it achieves a 2.0 mAP improvement over the prior state-of-the-art for a 2MB model and a 1.7 mAP gain for a 4MB model. These results confirm that Light-Student effectively enhances the performance of lightweight student networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/Cheng-Yu-Lin/Light-Student.

Bucket Elimination (BE) serves as a fundamental inference and optimization algorithm for graphical models, functioning as a generalization of variable elimination. While BE is optimal for inference and optimization tasks, its performance is constrained by the size of the factors it produces. This paper introduces a novel BE variant that leverages a specific class of factor decompositions known as $k$-decomposable functions. We demonstrate that this new approach, termed $k$-BE, is at least as effective as BE for both inference and optimization. Furthermore, we show that $k$-BE is optimal for inference when the $k$-decomposability of the optimal solution is bounded by a constant. Experimental results indicate that $k$-BE significantly outperforms BE in both inference and optimization tasks. Additionally, we introduce a new method for determining the optimal elimination ordering, which is crucial for both BE and $k$-BE. Our findings suggest that $k$-BE can be applied to problems that are currently intractable for BE. To facilitate the adoption of $k$-BE, we have implemented the algorithm and the new ordering method in a Python library called $k$-BE, which is available at https://github.com/GraphicalModelGroup/k-BE. The source code for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/GraphicalModelGroup/GraphicalModelGroup.github.io/blob/master/experiments/README.md.

The paired-permutation test serves as a nonparametric alternative to the paired t-test, offering a precise method for assessing statistical significance. However, its computational demands have historically hindered the adoption of exact p-values in large-scale analyses, such as genome-wide association studies. This paper introduces a novel exact algorithm that leverages a specific combinatorial structure to accelerate calculations. We demonstrate that this new approach is orders of magnitude faster than the Monte Carlo approximation, which is the standard method for estimating p-values in such contexts. Furthermore, we introduce a Monte Carlo variant of our exact algorithm, which combines the new exact procedure with a Monte Carlo strategy to generate a hybrid estimator. This hybrid method delivers an unbiased estimate of the p-value and achieves a lower mean squared error than the Monte Carlo approximation alone. Our findings indicate that the hybrid estimator is particularly effective for generating precise p-value estimates in scenarios involving small sample sizes or large effect sizes. To facilitate broader application, we have made the new exact algorithm and the hybrid estimator accessible via an R package, which is available at https://github.com/robertjames99/PPexact.

Our work focuses on accelerating the computation of the paired-permutation test, a nonparametric significance test used to evaluate the null hypothesis of no association between two variables. This test operates by permuting the values of one variable and recalculating the test statistic to generate a distribution of permuted statistics. The exact p-value is then determined by counting how many permuted statistics are at least as extreme as the observed statistic. While this approach is straightforward, it is computationally intensive, especially when dealing with large datasets or numerous tests. For instance, in genome-wide association studies, where millions of tests are conducted simultaneously, the computational burden becomes substantial. Consequently, researchers often rely on Monte Carlo approximations to estimate p-values, as these are significantly faster than calculating the exact value. Nevertheless, these approximations can be imprecise, particularly when the true p-value is small. In such cases, the Monte Carlo estimate may be biased upward, potentially leading to the failure to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false. This issue is especially critical in genome-wide association studies, where the focus is typically on identifying significant associations. To address this, we propose a new exact algorithm designed to accelerate the computation of the paired-permutation test. Additionally, we develop a Monte Carlo version of this exact algorithm to create a hybrid estimator that combines the benefits of both methods. This study introduces a reward model designed for the video game FIFA, trained using inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to derive game-theoretic optimal policies. The model's performance is evaluated through Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and Monte Carlo (MC) methods. Our approach involves training a neural network to predict rewards for specific state-action pairs, where states are represented by a combination of game features and a visual embedding derived from the game screen. We demonstrate that incorporating the visual embedding significantly enhances the reward model's performance. Furthermore, we show that the optimal policy identified by our reward model aligns with the actual actions taken by professional players. Finally, we compare the performance of MCTS and MC methods when utilizing our reward model against their traditional implementations. The results indicate that our reward model substantially improves the performance of both MCTS and MC approaches. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/chenyuxiang/FIFA-IRL.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm, Neural Best Response Fictitious Play (NBRFP), which integrates neural networks with best-response dynamics to address non-zero-sum games. Additionally, we demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in a large-scale non-zero-sum game, Poker, where the state space is vast. Our findings suggest that NBRFP can serve as a viable alternative to NashQ in such contexts. The source code for NBRFP is accessible at https://github.com/chenyuxiang/NBRFP.

For instance, the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC focus on NLLPs with decay lengths ranging from centimeters to meters, whereas the MoEDAL experiment targets macroscopic decay lengths. This paper introduces the concept of Bertrand curves within the framework of Finsler spaces, specifically examining their properties in $(n+1)$-dimensional spaces with $n \geq 2$. We establish that in $(n+1)$-dimensional Minkowski spaces where $n \geq 3$, Bertrand curves are impossible. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in $(n+1)$-dimensional Randers spaces with $n \geq 3$, the existence of Bertrand curves is limited to specific Randers metrics. Finally, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for a curve to be a Bertrand curve in $(n+1)$-dimensional Matsumoto spaces where $n \geq 3$. These findings extend the definition of Bertrand curves to various Finsler spaces, including $(n+1)$-dimensional Matsumoto spaces for $n \geq 2$. The results presented here are novel and significant.

This study introduces a novel approach to hyperparameter optimization for neural networks, specifically targeting under-represented loss functions such as the KL Divergence. We propose a new Bayesian optimization method called NeuralPareto, which utilizes a neural network to model the Pareto front of hyperparameters. Unlike traditional Bayesian optimization, NeuralPareto does not require the objective function to be differentiable. Our method employs a neural network to approximate the Pareto front, enabling the acquisition function to operate directly on this approximation. We evaluated NeuralPareto against state-of-the-art Bayesian optimization techniques using two distinct datasets. The results indicate that NeuralPareto outperforms existing methods, particularly for under-represented loss functions like the KL Divergence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the commonly used cross-entropy loss function can yield suboptimal performance compared to the KL Divergence. These findings suggest that the selection of a loss function is critical for achieving optimal results in neural network training. To support this, we release a comprehensive dataset of 100,000 optimized configurations for both the cross-entropy and KL Divergence losses, which is publicly available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1000/NeuralPareto. Our code is also open-sourced.

Neural models trained on the if-then structure of relation types achieve superior performance compared to those trained on flat type labels. This advantage is particularly evident when dealing with low-resource scenarios, where the scarcity of data for specific relation types hinders the learning of effective representations. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel multi-task learning framework designed to leverage the hierarchical organization of if-then relation types. Our approach involves two primary tasks: first, a multi-task learning model learns to predict the if-then type hierarchy for unseen sentence pairs; second, a fine-grained model utilizes the predicted if-then type to learn the corresponding fine-grained relation type. We apply this framework to the challenging FewShot Relation Classification (FRC) task, utilizing the ATOMIC dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art few-shot learning approaches. Furthermore, the model trained on the FRC task exhibits enhanced performance on the zero-shot RC task. These findings indicate that leveraging the if-then hierarchical structure of relation types is a viable strategy for improving few-shot learning in low-resource settings. To support this, we have made our code and the few-shot FRC dataset publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuan94/FewShotFRC.

We introduce a novel approach for predicting videos from unseen viewpoints, leveraging a dual representation that combines a view-independent encoding of scene geometry with a view-specific encoding of appearance. This framework enables the prediction of videos from novel viewpoints by integrating the view-independent geometric encoding with a new view-specific appearance encoding. To learn this dual representation, we utilize a large dataset of videos captured from multiple viewpoints. Our method employs a two-stage learning process: first, we train a view-independent encoder to extract a compact encoding of scene geometry from videos recorded across various viewpoints; second, we train a view-specific encoder to learn a compact encoding of appearance for a single novel viewpoint. The final prediction of videos from a new viewpoint is achieved by combining the view-independent geometric encoding with the view-specific appearance encoding. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets, HumanVid and UCF-101-VP, demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the HumanVid dataset without requiring any additional training data. These findings indicate that our approach can effectively predict videos from novel viewpoints using only a small set of videos from a single new viewpoint. Our dataset, model, and implementation are publicly available at https://github.com/ChenglongGuo/ViewPredictor.

We introduce a truncated metric, denoted as $d_{\tau}$, for graphs by limiting the standard geodesic distance $d$ to a specific threshold $\tau$. This modification creates a new metric space $(V, d_{\tau})$ that is no longer isometric to the original $(V, d)$. We examine the metric dimension of this truncated metric space, referred to as $dim_{\tau}(G)$. Our analysis reveals that $dim_{\tau}(G)$ remains constant for all $\tau$ exceeding a particular value, which we term the critical threshold, $t_{c}$. Furthermore, we establish that $t_{c}$ is bounded above by the metric dimension of the original graph, $dim(G)$. We derive an explicit formula for $t_{c}$ and provide a polynomial-time algorithm to calculate it. Additionally, we determine the exact value of $dim_{\tau}(G)$ for all $\tau$ when the graph is a tree. Finally, we explore the relationship between $t_{c}$ and the diameter of the graph. As a practical application, we demonstrate how this truncated metric can be utilized to identify the metric dimension of graphs with large diameters. The significance of this work lies in its potential to advance the study of metric spaces and their dimensions, offering valuable insights for graph theory and related fields. These findings could have implications for network analysis, data science, and other areas involving metric spaces. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of metric spaces and their dimensions, with potential applications across various disciplines.

This study introduces a novel approach to detect cardiac abnormalities in noisy settings by leveraging a pre-trained acoustic model. The method employs a two-stage framework: first, a pre-trained acoustic model extracts acoustic features from noisy heart sounds, which are then processed by a deep neural network (DNN) to identify anomalies. In the second stage, a pre-trained language model generates the final output. To enhance performance, we incorporated a pre-trained acoustic model into a two-stage system and introduced a pre-trained language model to refine the final results. Experimental findings indicate that this proposed method outperforms existing techniques in noisy environments. Specifically, the pre-trained acoustic model achieved a 1.5% increase in F1 score, while the pre-trained language model contributed a 1.2% improvement in F1 score. These results demonstrate that integrating pre-trained acoustic and language models into a two-stage framework significantly enhances the detection of cardiac abnormalities under noisy conditions. The proposed method offers a promising solution for identifying cardiac issues in environments with background noise, potentially benefiting medical professionals and patients alike. Furthermore, this approach could serve as a valuable tool for developing automated systems to detect cardiac abnormalities in noisy contexts. The source code is available at: https://github.com/AbdulWadood/Pretrained-Models-for-Noisy-Heart-Sound-Analysis.

We report the detection of the $^{13}$CO(1-0) line in the extreme starburst galaxy NGC 253 using the IRAM 30m telescope, representing the first identification of this transition in such a system. By combining this new measurement with existing data, we determined that the $^{13}$CO(1-0)/CO(1-0) ratio is approximately 0.01, a value consistent with the ratio of their integrated intensities. This finding indicates that the $^{13}$CO(1-0) emission originates from the same low-density molecular wind or circumgalactic gas reservoir responsible for the CI(1-0)/CO(1-0) ratio of roughly 0.01. Furthermore, we derived a molecular gas mass of $1.2\times10^{10}$ M$_{\odot}$, which aligns with the mass inferred from dust emission. These results suggest that the low CI/CO ratio in NGC 253 is not caused by optical depth effects in the CO(1-0) line, as previously hypothesized. Instead, the low CI/CO ratio likely arises because the CI(1-0) emission comes from a low-density reservoir that does not contribute to the CO(1-0) signal. Consequently, the CI(1-0) line serves as a valuable tracer for low-density molecular gas in extreme starburst galaxies. Additionally, we found that the ratio of CI(2-1) to CI(1-0) integrated intensities is approximately 0.5, implying that the CI(2-1) line is detectable in NGC 253 with current facilities. Finally, we observed that the CO(2-1)/CO(1-0) ratio is roughly 0.8, suggesting that the CO(2-1) line could be detected in NGC 253 with future instruments. These conclusions are applicable to other extreme starburst galaxies, including ULIRGs. The data presented here are available at https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...924...60S/abstract.

We examine the Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (ASEP) on the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}$, where particles follow a Bernoulli initial configuration with density $\alpha$. Focusing on the second class particle, we derive the exact distribution of its velocity at time $t$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, as $t$ approaches infinity, this velocity distribution converges to a Gaussian distribution with mean $q(\alpha-\frac{1}{2})$ and variance $\frac{1}{2}(\alpha(1-\alpha)+q^2)$. Additionally, we establish the convergence of the second class particle's trajectory to a Brownian motion with drift $q(\alpha-\frac{1}{2})$ and diffusion coefficient $\frac{1}{2}(\alpha(1-\alpha)+q^2)$. These findings extend the hydrodynamic limit of the ASEP to the second class particle, a result that is significant for understanding the behavior of other particle classes. Finally, we explore the connection between the second class particle and the $q$-Hahn polynomials. Our analysis reveals that the probability of finding a second class particle at a specific site at time $t$ can be expressed as a $q$-Hahn polynomial, which serves as the generating function for the velocity distribution. This relationship allows us to derive the exact velocity distribution from the particle's location distribution. Conversely, the hydrodynamic limit of the $q$-Hahn polynomials yields the Gaussian distribution for the velocity. These results are relevant to the study of integrable systems and stochastic processes.

Fitting differential models to data is a standard method for inferring epidemiological parameters, yet the resulting parameter values are often biologically unrealistic. This issue is particularly evident in models designed to fit the early phase of an epidemic, where data is limited and noisy. While this limitation is frequently overlooked, it can lead to misleading conclusions regarding the efficacy of interventions. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian approach that incorporates biological feasibility constraints into the fitting process. We demonstrate the application of this method using a detailed differential model for SARS-CoV-2 in the United States, which integrates data on infections, deaths, hospitalizations, and contact tracing. Our analysis reveals that the model's original parameter estimates were biologically infeasible. By enforcing biological feasibility constraints, we derived a new set of parameter estimates that are both biologically realistic and statistically consistent with the observed data. These revised estimates indicate that the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic in the US was driven by a combination of high transmissibility and insufficient social distancing measures. Furthermore, our findings suggest that contact tracing was ineffective in curbing the epidemic's spread. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of these results. To support reproducibility, the code used for this study is available at https://github.com/andrewjgibbs/BiologicalFeasibility.

We report the detection of a NUV-r color break in the mass distribution of galaxies at $z=0.7$, a phenomenon previously identified at $z=0$ by Brinchmann et al. (2010). This break signifies a shift in the NUV-r color for galaxies exceeding $M_* \sim 10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$, where the color becomes bluer with increasing mass. This trend is consistent with the findings of Brinchmann et al. (2010) at $z=0$. Furthermore, we observe that this break occurs at a lower mass threshold at higher redshifts, shifting from $M_* \sim 10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$ at $z=0.7$ to $M_* \sim 10^{10.8} M_{\odot}$ at $z=1.5$. Additionally, we find that the break in the NUV-r versus $M_*$ relation at $z=0.7$ aligns with the break in the $SFR/M_*$ relation, which marks the transition from star-forming to passive galaxies. These results suggest that the NUV-r color break at $z=0.7$ is primarily driven by the emergence of passive galaxies at high masses. Finally, we note that the NUV-r versus $M_*$ relation at $z=0.7$ exhibits a steeper slope than at $z=0$, indicating that the NUV-r color is more sensitive to $M_*$ at higher redshifts. This increased sensitivity is likely due to the greater influence of dust on the NUV-r color at $z=0.7$ compared to $z=0$. These findings imply that the NUV-r color is a more effective tracer of $SFR/M_*$ at $z=0.7$ than at $z=0$. Ultimately, our results suggest that the NUV-r color is a more reliable indicator of galaxy quenching at $z=0.7$ than at $z=0$. The data presented in this study are accessible at https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018arXiv180600605S/.

Multilingual sentiment analysis (MSA) is a significant natural language processing task that has attracted considerable attention in recent years. While numerous studies have focused on zero-shot MSA (ZS-MSA)—where models are trained on a single language and tested on multiple languages—there remains a scarcity of research on few-shot ZS-MSA, which involves training on a single language and testing on two languages, with only a small amount of data available for the target language. This paper introduces a new dataset, the Multilingual Twitter Sentiment Dataset (MTSD), designed for few-shot ZS-MSA. The MTSD comprises 1.5 million tweets in English, German, and Spanish, annotated with positive, negative, and neutral sentiments. We also introduce a novel few-shot ZS-MSA framework called Multi-Task Learning with Cross-lingual Auxiliary Tasks (MTL-CAT). In this approach, the model is trained on the source language and tested on both source and target languages, utilizing a small dataset from the target language as an auxiliary task. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed MTSD dataset and the MTL-CAT framework significantly outperform existing few-shot ZS-MSA methods. Furthermore, the MTSD dataset and the few-shot ZS-MSA task are publicly available at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/MTSD.

We report the detection of a 1.5-hour rotation period in the solar-like oscillating star KIC 9267654, a finding that contradicts the rotation profile typically observed among stars with similar fundamental parameters. To investigate these possibilities, we conducted a detailed analysis of the star's variability, spectral characteristics, and astrometric data. Our results indicate that KIC 9267654 is a single star with a mass of 1.20 $\pm$ 0.05 $M_{\odot}$ and a radius of 1.30 $\pm$ 0.05 $R_{\odot}$. These findings suggest that the unusual rotation is likely due to a recent merger, potentially resulting from a triple star system where a low-mass companion was accreted. To validate this hypothesis, we performed a Bayesian inference analysis using a hydrodynamical model of a merger between a 1.2 $M_{\odot}$ star and a 0.1 $M_{\odot}$ companion. The model successfully reproduced the star's variability, spectral features, and astrometric data, yielding a best-fit mass ratio of 0.08 $\pm$ 0.02. Consequently, we conclude that the merger between a 1.2 $M_{\odot}$ star and a 0.1 $M_{\odot}$ companion occurred approximately 10 Myr ago. This event likely caused the star's rotation to accelerate from a typical value of 0.5 km s$^{-1}$ to the current 11 km s$^{-1}$. Additionally, the merger may have generated the solar-like oscillations, as the hydrodynamical model aligns with the observed variability. This case represents the first instance where a merger has been identified as the cause of both rapid rotation and solar-like oscillations in a star. Fake news poses a significant threat to social media platforms, making the development of effective detection models essential. While existing models have achieved high accuracy, they often lack explainability, which is crucial for gaining user trust. To address this, we introduce MetaFEND, a novel end-to-end explainable model designed to detect fake news and generate corresponding explanations. Unlike prior approaches, MetaFEND integrates a multi-task learning framework with a hierarchical attention mechanism to simultaneously perform fake news detection and explanation generation. Furthermore, we introduce a new dataset, FEND, comprising 100,000 English news articles annotated with both labels and explanations. Experimental results demonstrate that MetaFEND outperforms current state-of-the-art models in both detection and explanation tasks. Additionally, the model's explainability has been validated through human evaluation. The FEND dataset and MetaFEND model are available at https://github.com/AbdulWaseem/FEND.

This study examines the feasibility of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs (GCAPs) with dimensions $N \times M$, where $N$ is an odd integer and $M$ is an even integer. It is demonstrated that for a quaternary Golay complementary array pair of size $N \times M$ to exist, the product $NM$ must satisfy the congruence $NM \equiv 0, 1, 4 \pmod{12}$. Furthermore, it is proven that quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of size $5 \times 2m$ exist for all even integers $m \geq 2$. Finally, the paper establishes the existence of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs with dimensions $7 \times 2m$ for all even integers $m \geq 2$. These findings are derived using a constructive approach. The results indicate that the feasible sizes for quaternary Golay complementary array pairs are more extensive than those for quaternary Golay complementary sequences. Additionally, the existence of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of size $N \times M$ (where $N$ is odd and $M$ is even) implies the existence of quaternary Golay complementary sequences of length $NM$. This suggests that the feasible sizes for quaternary Golay complementary sequences are also broader than previously documented. To validate these conclusions, explicit constructions of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs for sizes $5 \times 2m$ and $7 \times 2m$ (with $m \geq 2$) are provided. These constructions rely on a specific method for generating quaternary Golay complementary sequences of length $4k+1$ (where $k \geq 1$) and a construction technique for quaternary Golay complementary array pairs of size $3 \times 2m$ (where $m \geq 2$). The explicit constructions for sizes $5 \times 2m$ and $7 \times 2m$ ($m \geq 2$) are detailed in Sections 3 and 4, respectively. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these results.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become a standard approach for segmenting regions of interest in medical images, particularly for tasks involving the identification of anatomical structures and pathological areas. This paper introduces a novel CNN architecture designed to segment both anatomical and pathological regions within brain MRI scans. The proposed model integrates a multi-scale feature extraction module with a multi-task learning framework to simultaneously address anatomical and pathological segmentation. To enhance feature extraction, the architecture incorporates a multi-scale feature extraction module and a multi-scale attention mechanism. Dynamical systems are mathematical frameworks used to model the evolution of physical systems over time. These systems are categorized into two primary types: discrete and continuous. In a discrete dynamical system, the state at any given time is determined by the state at the preceding time step. Conversely, in a continuous dynamical system, the state at any moment is influenced by the state at an infinitesimally prior moment. The Lyapunov exponent is a metric employed to assess the stability of dynamical systems. A positive Lyapunov exponent signifies chaotic behavior, whereas a negative value indicates stability. This metric is particularly valuable for analyzing chaotic systems, such as the Lorenz system, which exhibits chaotic dynamics. The Lyapunov exponent is defined as the limit of the logarithm of the ratio of the lengths of two initially close trajectories as time approaches infinity. Specifically, if $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ represent two trajectories originating from nearby initial conditions $x_0$ and $y_0$, the Lyapunov exponent $\lambda$ is expressed as:

$$\lambda = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t} \ln \left( \frac{\|x(t) - y(t)\|}{\|x_0 - y_0\|} \right).$$

When $\lambda > 0$, the system is considered chaotic; when $\lambda < 0$, it is stable; and when $\lambda = 0$, the system is neutrally stable. This is primarily due to the difficulty of integrating backdoor behaviors into models during inference, a challenge that has hindered the development of effective dynamic backdoor attacks across various classification tasks. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for dynamic backdoor attacks in multi-label classification. We validate DynamicB's effectiveness through extensive experiments on two real-world multi-label datasets and two standard benchmark datasets. Results demonstrate that DynamicB achieves a significant reduction in F1-score compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we confirm that the dynamic backdoor generated by DynamicB remains undetectable under both white-box and black-box detection scenarios. Federated learning enables the training of models across distributed data sources without requiring data centralization, yet it often suffers from communication inefficiencies due to the high volume of data involved. This paper introduces a novel random walk approach designed to mitigate these inefficiencies. By leveraging a random walk strategy, the proposed method reduces the number of communication rounds needed to achieve a specific accuracy level. We validate this approach through a case study on a learning-from-examples task, demonstrating that the random walk technique significantly lowers communication costs compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric to quantify the efficiency of various strategies in reducing communication. The findings indicate that the random walk approach is particularly effective for tasks involving a large number of examples, offering substantial communication savings. Ultimately, this work presents a viable solution for enhancing the efficiency of federated learning systems. Our approach is applicable to any learning-from-examples scenario, including those utilizing one-shot or few-shot learning techniques.

1. Define the learning-from-examples task and the associated data distribution.
2. Select a random walk strategy to optimize communication.

The effectiveness of this approach is best understood through a concrete example. Consider a scenario where Alice and Bob aim to train a model on their respective datasets, $D_A$ and $D_B$, to classify images into categories such as "cat" or "dog." This iterative exchange of examples and models continues until the model $f(x)$ reaches the desired accuracy. This random walk method allows Alice and Bob to train an effective model without ever transmitting their complete data distributions.

Extensive experiments conducted on three medical image segmentation datasets confirm that our approach effectively enhances model robustness against data noise. These results suggest that IM is a valuable regularization strategy for SSL in medical image segmentation, particularly when dealing with noisy, unannotated data.
